SILIGURI CAGE: LOGGER ON THE SHELF - WHEN THE BATTERY GETS CHANGED

A USB logger sitting on the cage shelf has its battery changed every 12 months,
whatever its sticker says.

MINIMUM UNCONDITIONED BLUE-CAP PACKS

The cage keeps at least 30 unconditioned blue-cap packs at all times, which is
enough to remake two shippers.

Count both items every Friday.

## 6. Spare instruments

6.1. Stores holds spare hand-held probes and spare USB loggers for issue, but
does not decide whether an instrument is fit to use. The sticker, put on by QA,
decides that.

6.2. A spare logger's battery is replaced by Stores after 24 months on the
shelf, whatever the logger's sticker says, and the logger then goes back to the
QA bench before it can be issued.

6.3. An instrument with a yellow sticker may be issued. An instrument with a red
sticker or red tape is never issued and goes back to QA.

6.4. Stores keeps a list of every instrument by its prefix number and the date
of its last in-house check, so that QA can see what is due.

6.5. Instruments sent to the external lab are packed by QA and handed to the
courier by Stores. Stores records the date they left and the date they came
back.

## 10. Counting

10.1. Stores counts seals, sleeves and instruments every Friday, and everything
else at the month end.

10.2. A count is done by two people, one of whom did not issue anything that
week.

10.3. At the Friday count the logger shelf is checked by date: a logger whose
last bench check is more than 90 days old is moved to the QA tray, and a logger
whose battery date shows more than 24 months is flagged, but nothing in the
store count replaces what the QA bench decides.

10.4. Differences are written up the same day and sent to Nalini Patil. A
difference in seals or loggers is reported to QA and Fleet Control as well.

10.5. Guwahati and Coimbatore cages send their counts to the Nagpur store by
email on the first working day of the month.

## 5. Instruments that travel south

5.1. Coimbatore has no calibration chamber and no bench master logger. Those
live at Nagpur. What Coimbatore does have is one lab-certified hand-held
thermometer, serial HP-C00, kept locked in the DC manager's cabinet.

5.2. Every hand-held thermometer in daily use at Coimbatore is checked against
HP-C00 every 14 days: both tips go into the same stirred jug of crushed ice and
water, and the two readings must agree within 0.5 C. The shift lead writes both
readings on QCL-F-12 and sends a photograph of the sheet to the Nagpur QA desk.

5.3. The shorter interval is deliberate. Coimbatore has no bench to catch a
drifting instrument quickly, and a second jug check costs nothing but ten
minutes.

5.4. HP-C00 itself goes to Metrosure Labs, Pune, by courier every 12 months.
While it is away, the Nagpur QA desk sends a loan instrument ahead of it, so the
site is never without a certified thermometer.

5.5. USB loggers are not checked at Coimbatore at all. Every spare logger for a
Coimbatore red sleeve is checked at the Nagpur bench and arrives in its sleeve
already stickered. A logger that has been out of date on the shelf is sent back
to Nagpur, never re-used on the strength of a local jug check.

5.6. Infrared guns are used at Coimbatore only to find a warm carton quickly.
They are never the reading that decides anything.

## 3. Getting a vehicle in and out

3.1. Reefers use the south gate. The east gate is for dry grocery only unless
the DC manager approves an emergency move, as the old wiki page also said.

3.2. School traffic on Temple Street blocks the turn into the south gate between
07:45 and 08:30. Drivers are told on booking to arrive either before 07:30 or
after 08:40. A reefer is never queued across Temple Street; if the apron is
full, the driver goes round the block and comes back.

3.3. Security holds each vehicle outside the south gate until the previous one
has cleared the apron. The apron takes one reefer and one van at a time, no
more, because a reversing reefer cannot see a second one parked behind it.

3.4. Bookings are made in Dockwise, which Coimbatore joined on 1 February 2026.
The grace table and the cancellation rule are the company rule, not a local
one, and are not repeated here.

3.5. Frozen loads are placed before lunch. After about 13:00 the afternoon sun
lies across the outer apron, drivers open their doors to check paperwork, and
the frozen body loses cold it cannot spare.

3.6. Reversing on the apron after dark needs a spotter with a torch, whatever
the vehicle's camera shows. The apron lights are on a timer that the landlord
controls, and they have twice failed to come on in the monsoon.

## 5. Red sleeve packets

5.1. Stores holds red sleeve packets empty. QA makes each packet up, including a
spare logger checked at the bench, before it is issued.

5.2. A made-up packet comes back to Stores from QA sealed with a tamper label.
Stores does not open it.

5.3. Stores issues made-up packets to DCs and to reefer cab lockers against a
signature. A packet returned unused and unopened goes back on the shelf; a
packet returned opened goes to QA to be made up again.

5.4. Stores keeps at least ten made-up packets at Nagpur at all times. When the
stock falls to ten, Stores tells QA in writing.

5.5. Packets ordered under the red sleeve project are recorded against that
project's budget line, not against the Stores consumables line.

## 24. Review of this standard

24.1. Nalini Patil reviews this standard every July with QA and Finance, and
sooner when a new consumable is introduced or a supplier changes.

24.2. A change to how an item is used is made in the document that governs its
use, not here. This standard changes only how Stores receives, holds, issues and
counts the item.

24.3. Each revision is issued with a note of what changed. The storekeepers at
Nagpur and the cage leads at Guwahati and Coimbatore sign that they have read it
within a week.

24.4. The earlier revision is withdrawn from the Stores counter and the shared
drive on the day the new one is issued, so that nobody works from two versions
at the same time.

# Stores and Consumables Standard

How Stores receives, holds and issues the consumables that cold-chain work runs
on: seals, red sleeve packets, spare loggers, gel packs, dry ice, protective
equipment and forms. It covers the main store at Nagpur and the smaller stores
cages at Guwahati and Coimbatore. It does not say how any of these items is used
on the job; the documents that govern their use do that.

# Quillfern Cold Chain Glossary

Plain meanings for expressions used on site. Short forms are defined in the document that uses them, never here, so an expression below appears in its long form only.

back-to-cold — the moment a staged pallet crosses back over the cold-room threshold; staging time stops here.
chlorine contact time — the minutes a sanitising solution must stay wet on a reefer floor before rinsing; wiping it dry early starts the count again.
dead zone — a stretch of road where the telematics unit cannot report; the USB logger covers it and the gap is recorded as missing, never filled in.
door open minutes — the total minutes a cold-room or reefer door stood open in one shift, summed from the door sensor; a measure of load, not a fault.
holding lane B — the covered waiting lane at Nagpur for pharma and frozen vehicles that miss their dock time; nothing is unloaded there.
mean kinetic temperature — the single steady temperature that would give stock the same total heat stress as the uneven record it actually saw; stability letters are written against it, not against the average.
pre-cool hold time — the minutes an empty reefer body is held at loading temperature, doors shut, before the first pallet goes in.
probe grid — the layout of loggers used when a room is mapped; each position is named by rack, bay and height, such as A1-high.
relief point — a named fuel plaza or rest area on a qualified route where a relief driver or a mobile service van can meet the vehicle.
seal watch — time a driver spends guarding a sealed vehicle; it is duty time and never counts as rest.
shipper conditioning time — the hours a passive shipper's gel packs must sit at their set temperature before the shipper may leave with stock.
stability budget remaining — the minutes above the high limit that a customer's stability letter still allows for one lot, once every earlier excursion on that lot is subtracted.
warm pallet — night-shift name for a pallet whose logger has alarmed but whose excursion QA has not yet confirmed; it is handled as quarantine stock until QA decides.
white tag — the RELEASED tag fixed beside a red hold tag when QA lets stock out of quarantine; the red tag stays on.

## 1. Release

1.1. Release is recorded on form QCL-F-31 and signed by the QA investigator and a second QA officer who did not investigate the case.

1.2. A white RELEASED tag is fixed beside the red hold tag. The red hold tag is never removed; both stay on the stock until it leaves the site.

1.3. Stock is not released between 22:00 and 06:00, whatever the dispatch plan says. The earliest release of the day is at 06:00.

1.4. Released quantity is counted twice by two people and entered separately from any destroyed quantity.

# Quarantine Stock Release and Return Procedure

How stock leaves quarantine bays Q-3 (Nagpur), Q-G2 (Guwahati) and Q-C1 (Coimbatore) after QA has recorded a disposition under clause 6.5 of the [Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). Destroyed stock does not leave by this procedure; section 7 of that SOP governs it.

## 2. The Fleet Control desk

2.1. Fleet Control sits at Nagpur DC and answers extension 301 at all hours. At
night one controller is on duty, with the Fleet head's deputy on call.

2.2. Fleet Control owns the dispatch note, the vehicle's route and the driver's
duty plan. A shift lead can hold a vehicle at the gate, but only Fleet Control
can change a route or a driver.

2.3. Every call from a driver is logged in the driver call log with the time,
the place and what was said, including calls that come to nothing. The paper
log is kept alongside the Tessaline record because network coverage is patchy
on several lanes.

2.4. Fleet Control does not pass customer pressure to a driver. A customer who
wants a location or an arrival time asks customer service, and customer service
asks Fleet Control.

2.5. Each controller hands over at 08:00 and 20:00, with every open exception,
every vehicle on the road with a pharma critical load, and every vehicle off
road for repair named aloud.

## 9. Insulated boxes in the load

9.1. A validated passive shipper carries pharma stock inside a reefer body or on
a body without a cradle, such as RF-119.

9.2. A closed shipper is validated for 48 hours from the lid-closing time
written in the shipper register. A shipper that will still be on the road at 40
hours is called in to Fleet Control, and QA decides whether it is re-packed or
the consignment is held.

9.3. The shipper's lid is never opened on the road. The tamper label across the
lid seam is photographed at departure and again at delivery.

9.4. Shippers travel upright, strapped to the body wall, and never under other
freight.

9.5. The empty shipper comes back on the return run in the same condition it
went out, with its packs inside and its logger taped in place, so that QA can
download the logger and count the pack cycles.

## 12. Paperwork that comes back

12.1. Each trip returns a trip bag holding the dispatch note, the fuel slips,
the cut seals, the takeover sheet and any exception form.

12.2. The trip bag is handed to the shift lead at the returning DC, who checks
it against the dispatch note and signs for it.

12.3. A missing item in the trip bag is written on the dispatch note as
missing, never replaced with a guess. A torn fuel slip is kept torn.

12.4. Trip bags from a trip involving a tyre change or other vendor work carry
the vendor's job sheet with the hours and the spare parts used, so that Fleet
Control can match it to the vendor's invoice.

12.5. Trip bags are kept by Fleet Control for three years, or seven where the
trip involved a pharma critical excursion, a crash, an insurance claim or a
police matter.

# Taloja freezer store card: blast cell, order cut-off, gas leak siren

Pinned at the Taloja order desk. This card covers three things: the arrival
probe and the blast cell, the order cut-off for next-day vans, and where to
line up when the gas leak siren sounds.

## 7. The plant room

7.1. The site is cooled by a carbon dioxide refrigeration rack. The plant room
holds the compressors, the receiver and the gas cooler, and the gas cooler's
fans sit on the roof above it.

7.2. Gas detectors in the plant room, in FC-A and in the cell watch for leaks. A
first stage lights the amber beacon over the plant room door and calls the plant
lead. A second stage sounds the site siren.

7.3. Only the plant lead and the refrigeration contractor's technician enter the
plant room. Both carry a personal gas monitor clipped to the chest.

7.4. When the leak siren sounds, forklifts stop where they are, engines are
switched off and nobody goes back for stock, a phone or a vehicle. Everyone walks to BW-A, the painted square beside the truck scale, and stays there until the plant lead clears the site in person.

7.5. The shift lead counts heads against the gate log and the contract labour
sheet within ten minutes and phones the count to the site manager. Drivers
waiting on the apron are counted by the guard.

7.6. A siren test is run on the first Monday of every month at 11:00, announced
the day before. Nobody leaves the building for a test.

7.7. The refrigeration contractor services the rack every quarter and after any
leak alarm. The service sheet is kept in the plant room folder and copied to the
site manager.

# Ammonia alarm at Nagpur: what to do

## When the site siren sounds

1. Stop forklifts and trucks where they are and switch the engines off. Nobody drives through the plant yard.
2. Leave by the nearest door that does not face the compressor house. The security guard brings the gate register.
3. Go to muster point M2 by gate 2, beside the windsock.
4. The shift lead counts heads against the gate register and the dock sheet within 10 minutes and phones the count to the plant operator on extension 215.
5. Nobody goes back for stock, a phone or a truck. Pallets left on a dock are dealt with afterwards under QCL-QA-SOP-17; product loss is a QA matter.

## 2. Building, bays and who is where

2.1. The shed is a single span with six dock doors on the east wall, numbered D1
to D6 from the gate side. D1 and D2 take incoming trailers, D3 opens into the
cell behind it, and D4 to D6 load outgoing vans.

2.2. The freezer chamber FC-A runs at -22 C and holds 1,140 pallet positions in
drive-in racking. The marshalling anteroom in front of it is held at +4 C so
that cartons being picked for vans do not collect frost.

2.3. The plant room is on the north side, outside the insulated envelope, with
its own door to the yard. The office is on a mezzanine above D1 and D2, with a
window over the dock so that the order desk can see what is being unloaded.

2.4. The truck scale is at the gate, on the left as a vehicle enters, and every
inbound trailer is weighed in and out. The guard cabin is beside the scale.

2.5. Battery charging for the reach trucks is in a fenced bay outside the
anteroom. Nobody charges a truck inside FC-A, and nobody leaves a battery on
charge unattended across a shift change.

2.6. The canteen and lockers are in a single-storey block beside the gate.
Drivers waiting for a dock may use the canteen. They may not walk past the
yellow line painted along the dock edge.

2.7. The first-aid room is next to the canteen. The nearest hospital with a
casualty department is on the Kalyan road, about 7 km away; the route is
printed on the back of the first-aid room door.

## Door ajar alarm

If the door is left ajar, the PVF-200 beeps after 60 seconds and rings the
on-call engineer after 5 minutes.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 1. The six units

1.1. The pool owns six units, MCR-1 to MCR-6. Each is a 20-foot insulated
container with a refrigeration unit at one end, a personnel door at the other,
internal shelving and a controller that logs the inside temperature every
minute.

1.2. MCR-1 to MCR-4 run at +2 to +8 C and are used for chilled medicine and
chilled food. MCR-5 and MCR-6 can also run at -20 C and are used for frozen
stock or for vaccines that are shipped frozen.

1.3. At any time about four units are out on campaign hires of a few weeks and
two are on long hires. The pool coordinator keeps the deployment board.

1.4. Every unit carries its number on both long sides and on the door. A unit is
never relabelled, even after a refurbishment.

1.5. The units were bought in 2024 and 2025. Their refrigeration units are under
the maker's warranty until the dates written on the inside of each door.

## If the monitor beeps

If the CO2 monitor over the chest beeps, leave the room, shut the door and call the shift lead.

## 9. The engineer's calendar

9.1. Every unit has a compressor hour meter. Every 1,000 hours on the compressor meter, or every four months if that comes first, the unit gets a full visit.

9.2. A full visit covers the refrigerant charge, the condenser coil, the fans,
the door seal, the heaters, the drain, the controller probe and the alarm call.

9.3. The engineer writes the meter reading and the work done on the unit's
service card, which hangs inside the door, and in the pool's own log.

9.4. A unit that misses a visit is taken off hire at the end of its current
booking until the visit is done.

9.5. Controller probes are checked against a calibrated reference at every full
visit.

## 10. Alarms and the duty phone

10.1. The controller calls the duty phone for a high or low temperature, a door
left open, a power failure and a controller fault.

10.2. The pool engineer on duty answers the duty phone at all hours and calls
back the customer's lead within 15 minutes.

10.3. A temperature alarm is handled under the company's excursion rules. The
customer's staff do not move stock out of the unit unless the engineer tells
them to.

10.4. Each alarm and its outcome are written in the pool's alarm log.

lends out.

## 5. Instruments that travel south

5.1. Coimbatore has no calibration chamber and no bench master logger. Those
live at Nagpur. What Coimbatore does have is one lab-certified hand-held
thermometer, serial HP-C00, kept locked in the DC manager's cabinet.

5.2. Every hand-held thermometer in daily use at Coimbatore is checked against
HP-C00 every 14 days: both tips go into the same stirred jug of crushed ice and
water, and the two readings must agree within 0.5 C. The shift lead writes both
readings on QCL-F-12 and sends a photograph of the sheet to the Nagpur QA desk.

5.3. The shorter interval is deliberate. Coimbatore has no bench to catch a
drifting instrument quickly, and a second jug check costs nothing but ten
minutes.

5.4. HP-C00 itself goes to Metrosure Labs, Pune, by courier every 12 months.
While it is away, the Nagpur QA desk sends a loan instrument ahead of it, so the
site is never without a certified thermometer.

5.5. USB loggers are not checked at Coimbatore at all. Every spare logger for a
Coimbatore red sleeve is checked at the Nagpur bench and arrives in its sleeve
already stickered. A logger that has been out of date on the shelf is sent back
to Nagpur, never re-used on the strength of a local jug check.

5.6. Infrared guns are used at Coimbatore only to find a warm carton quickly.
They are never the reading that decides anything.

## Handheld thermometer checks

Every handheld thermometer in daily use at Hosur is checked against the
certified thermometer every 7 days, in a stirred jug of ice and water. The two
readings must agree within 0.5 C.

# Hosur depot card: handheld thermometer checks, dry ice totes, CO2 monitor over the chest

For the Hosur depot in Tamil Nadu. This card covers how often handheld
thermometers are checked, when a dry ice tote needs two people, and the CO2
monitor over the dry ice chest.

# Probe calibration: terms and tolerances

## Terms

- **ice point** — 0.0 C, the temperature of a stirred slurry of crushed ice and potable water.
- **bench master** — the lab-certified logger kept in the QA calibration chamber at Nagpur, serial UL-M01, recertified every 12 months by Metrosure Labs.
- **drift** — the change in an instrument's error between two checks.
- **pass band** — the largest error an instrument may show and still be used.

## 9. Insulin without spare cold

9.1. Coimbatore holds no passive shippers, no gel packs and no conditioning
cabinet. The passive shipper pilot is at Nagpur only, and it does not extend to
Coimbatore until a later project is approved.

9.2. Because there are no shippers, insulin at Coimbatore is never staged on an
open dock beyond the SOP limit. Insulin moves from CBE-PHARMA straight into a
reefer body that is already at loading temperature, and the reefer waits for
the insulin, never the other way round.

9.3. A customer who asks Coimbatore for a shipper-packed consignment is told
that the site cannot pack one. The account manager may arrange for a
shipper-packed consignment to come from Nagpur.

9.4. Coimbatore does not stock blue-cap or white-cap packs of any kind, and does
not freeze packs in CBE-FROZEN for customers. A customer's own packs returned
with a consignment go back with the customer's return challan.

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

## Notes on the lab

Drift is normal in cheap probes and is the main reason the bench exists. Monthly
figures are kept on QCL-F-12 so that a trend can be seen. External labs issue
one certificate per instrument, which QA files against the prefix number. An
instrument that passed at the lab still needs its in-house check when it comes
back.

## When a restaurant freezer fails: dry ice quantity billed

When a Tandoor Junction restaurant's freezer fails, we pack dry ice for it. The
quantity billed is at least 5 kg per request, whatever smaller quantity the
restaurant asks for.

## 10. Emergency cold for a customer's kitchen

10.1. Restaurant chains sometimes ask for emergency dry-ice packing when their
own freezer fails. Customer service takes the request; the DC decides whether it
can be done.

10.2. The agent does not promise a time. The DC tells the agent when the packing
can be ready, and the agent passes that on.

10.3. Emergency dry-ice packing is billed at a minimum of 10 kg per request,
whatever smaller quantity the kitchen asks for, and the per-kg price is the one
on the rate card in force.

10.4. Dry ice is never sent in a customer's own car unless the customer's driver
signs the dry-ice safety note at the gate. Customer service sends the note to
the customer with the confirmation.

10.5. Pharma customers are not offered dry-ice packing as an emergency measure.

The pilot met its acceptance tests. The C2 sensor tracked the USB logger within

Kalpa's five-minute polling required interpolation in every investigation
timeline. Sixty-second polling removed that argument from three customer
disputes in the first quarter of parallel running.

The local-service argument that carried the 2023 decision no longer holds.
Tessaline's Nagpur field team replaced two truck devices within one working day
during the January 2026 cold wave.

Polling is 60 seconds. The approved export is exception_csv_v2. Trip references
now use the TSL prefix; the KLP prefix is retained only for audit packets
covering trips before 18 August 2025.

IT retires the Kalpa export script on 30 April 2026. The Kalpa tablet in the
Nagpur guard cabin is a read-only audit device and must not be used to open
alarms. Training material and the QA audit binder are reissued with Tessaline
screenshots before the 2026 vaccine season.

Fleet continues to keep paper driver call logs. That practice survived the
vendor change because network coverage, not the vendor, was the reason for it.

# Telematics Vendor Decision 2026

Status: Accepted

## Context

The 2023 decision renewed Kalpa Fleet Systems for 36 months from 1 January 2024.
That decision is retired by this record. The cutover thread of July to September
2025 moved Quillfern to Tessaline Telematics for operational data, but no
decision record was ever written, and three audits asked why the accepted record
on file still named a vendor we no longer use.

This record states the present position so that no auditor, trainer, or new
manager has to read an email chain to learn which vendor is current.

## 9. Wood in, wood out

9.1. Pallets at the site are exchanged one for one. A trailer that brings in
twenty-two loaded pallets takes away twenty-two empty ones, so that neither side
ends up holding the other's wood.

9.2. Pallets are counted at the dock when a trailer is unloaded and again when
the empties are loaded. Both counts go on the pallet sheet and are signed by the
driver and the shift lead.

9.3. Every pallet handed in is looked at on the dock by the shift lead: split
boards, cracked blocks and missing nails are the usual faults. Each one that cannot carry a load is billed back at Rs. 450 to whoever delivered it.

9.4. Damaged pallets are stacked by the south fence for the repairer, who
collects on the first and third Fridays of each month. Repaired pallets come
back into the exchange pool; pallets that cannot be repaired are sold as scrap.

9.5. A driver who disputes a damaged-pallet count photographs the pallet before
leaving, and the office reviews the photograph against the shift lead's note.

9.6. Pallets are never used as dunnage in a van, never burned on site and never
given away, however broken.

## 1. Parties and how to read this

1.1. The parties are Quillfern Cold Logistics Pvt. Ltd. ("Quillfern") and
Saptagiri Foods Pvt. Ltd. ("the customer"), a maker of frozen parathas, samosas
and snacks with a factory at Chakan.

1.2. The agreement began on 1 April 2025 and runs until either side ends it under section 10.

1.3. Amendment 1 took effect on 1 October 2025 and changed the payment terms.
Amendment 2 took effect on 1 April 2026 and changed the liability cap. Both are
folded into the text below and listed in section 15.

1.4. Clause numbers here follow this consolidation, not the original agreement.
A clause quoted from the signed record carries its original number.

## 2. The work

2.1. Quillfern collects the customer's frozen products from the Chakan factory,
stores them and delivers them to restaurants, caterers and retailers in Pune
and Mumbai.

2.2. Pune deliveries go out from Quillfern's own stock. Mumbai-bound stock is
cross-docked at Quillfern's Bhiwandi site and goes out on the next morning's
vans.

2.3. Call-off times for Mumbai deliveries are those printed in the site handbook of the cross-dock that ships them.

2.4. Waiting charges on the customer's own vehicles at the cross-dock are billed at the site's published rate less 20 per cent.

2.5. Pallets are exchanged one for one at the cross-dock. Exchange units that arrive unfit on the customer's own vehicles are charged at the site figure, with no discount.

2.6. Quillfern does not sell, promote or price the customer's products and does
not take orders from the customer's buyers directly.

## 10. Ending the agreement

10.1. Either side may bring it to an end by giving 120 days' written notice.

10.2. Either side may end it at once if the other fails to pay, or fails to
perform a material obligation, and does not put it right within 30 days of a
written demand.

10.3. On ending, Quillfern returns the customer's stock to Chakan or to a place
the customer names in Pune, at the customer's cost, within 15 days.

## 5. Temperatures

5.1. The customer's products are kept at -18 C or colder in storage and in
transit.

5.2. The customer pre-cools each trailer before loading at Chakan and sends the
pre-cool record with the trailer.

5.3. Product that turns up above minus 12 is brought down to temperature at the cross-dock, and that work is invoiced to the customer.

5.4. Quillfern is not liable for product damage caused by temperatures before
handover. Each party may inspect the other's temperature records for its
stock.

## 4. Product, packing and handover

4.1. The customer packs its products in cartons that carry the batch number and
the best-before date on two faces.

4.2. Loaded pallets stand no higher than 1.8 metres including the wooden base. Taller pallets are restacked at the customer's cost before they are
accepted.

4.3. Each pallet is stretch-wrapped and labelled with the customer's pallet ID
on two faces.

4.4. Handover takes place when the pallet crosses the dock edge at the
receiving site. The receiving shift lead's count is the count.

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

## 14. Paper we keep

14.1. The gate log, the inbound sheets, the cell log, the pallet sheets, the van

14.2. Records about a pallet that was held, destroyed or disputed are kept for
seven years, with the photographs.

14.3. Paper sheets are scanned at the end of each week and filed in the site
folder. The paper originals go to the archive room in the office.

14.4. A missing sheet is written as missing in the weekly scan index, never
rewritten from memory.

## 4. Behind door 3

4.1. The cell behind D3 is BC-1, a blast cell with an air temperature of -35 C
and room for six pallets. It exists because brand owners do not always send
stock as cold as their paperwork says, and a frozen store is not built to pull
warm stock down; it is built to hold cold stock cold.

4.2. Every inbound pallet is probed at the dock: one carton from the middle of
the pallet, probe into the product core. Anything with a core warmer than minus 12 on the arrival probe goes behind door 3 first, whatever the paperwork says.

4.3. The target in the cell is a core of minus 18. It gets six hours from the moment the doors close. A load that has not reached target by then is reported to QA and held, and the customer is told the same day.

4.4. Stock that comes out of the cell is probed again before it goes into FC-A,
and both readings are written on the inbound sheet with their times.

4.5. The cell is never used as overflow storage, however busy the night. A
pallet parked in the cell because FC-A is full blocks the next soft arrival,
and the next soft arrival then sits on the dock warming further.

4.6. The cell's fans put a hard frost on cartons that sit too close to the coil.
Pallets are placed on the painted floor marks and nowhere else.

4.7. Whether cell time is charged depends on the customer's contract, not on
this handbook. The shift lead records the door-closing and door-opening times on
the cell log so that the office can apply whatever the contract says.

4.8. The cell was enlarged from four to six pallet places in March 2026. The two
extra places took space from the apron, which is why the apron now holds nine
vehicles and not eleven.

## 8. When the grid drops

8.1. The site has two gensets on a common panel. They start automatically when
grid power fails and carry FC-A, the cell, the plant room and the apron lights.
The canteen and the office air conditioning are not on the genset panel.

8.2. The gensets are test-run under load every Thursday at 10:00 for twenty
minutes. The run time, the oil level and any alarm on the panel are written in
the genset log.

8.3. The gensets share one day tank and one bulk tank. The tank is never allowed below 1,500 litres; the night lead dips it at 22:00 and orders a top-up from the listed bowser at 2,500.

8.4. During a long outage the night lead dips the tank every four hours and
writes each reading in the log. A bowser that does not arrive within four hours
of an order is chased by the site manager, not by the night lead.

8.5. Nobody refuels a genset while it is running. Fuel spills are covered with
the sand from the bin beside the tank and reported the same shift.

8.6. After the grid returns, the gensets run on for ten minutes before they are
shut down, and the panel is checked for any alarm that was raised during the
outage.

## 7. When things go wrong

7.1. Quillfern is liable for loss of or damage to the customer's products while

7.2. For any single pallet the ceiling is Rs. 25,000, and the total for a contract year is Rs. 40 lakh.

7.3. Amendment 2 raised it from Rs. 18,000 with effect from 1 April 2026. The
contract-year total was not changed.

7.4. Neither party is liable to the other for lost profit or for loss of
business.

7.5. A claim is made in writing within 30 days of the event, with photographs
and the count records.

18.1. Customer contact details are kept in the customer service system only. They

18.2. A customer's prices, volumes and incident history are not shared with any

18.3. Recordings of calls are kept for ninety days unless a ticket needs them for

18.4. A request from a customer to see the data Quillfern holds on them goes to
the account manager and to Pune HQ's legal contact on the day it arrives.

## 16. Tolls and road charges

16.1. Every owned reefer carries an electronic toll tag registered to Quillfern.
The tag balance is topped up by Fleet Control; drivers never pay a toll in cash
unless the tag reader at the plaza has failed.

16.2. A cash toll is paid only against a printed receipt, which goes into the
trip bag. A handwritten receipt is accepted only when the plaza staff sign and
stamp it.

16.3. A tag that shows a low balance at a plaza is reported to Fleet Control
while parked, and Fleet Control tops it up before the next plaza.

16.4. Hired trucks use their own tags. Quillfern does not refund a hired truck's
tolls unless the purchase order says so.

16.5. Road charges at state borders and permit fees are paid by Fleet Control in
advance for owned reefers. A driver asked for money at a border that was not on
the dispatch note calls Fleet Control before paying anything.

## 7. When the doors are opened on the road

7.1. Police, excise, sales tax and transport officers may stop a loaded reefer
and ask to see the load. Drivers cooperate, and do not argue about cold chain
at the roadside.

7.2. The driver asks for the officer's name and badge number and writes both on
the back of the dispatch note, with the time and place. The driver photographs
the seal before it is cut, if the officer allows.

7.3. After the inspection the driver fits a fresh bolt seal from the road pack
of five kept in the cab locker, writes the new number beside the old one on the
dispatch note, and photographs it. The cut seal goes into the trip bag.

7.4. The driver then phones Fleet Control on extension 301, while parked, and
Fleet Control enters both seal numbers in QCL-F-35 against the trip.

7.5. If the inspection kept the doors open for more than a few minutes on a
pharma critical load, Fleet Control tells QA, and the minutes are part of the
temperature record like any other door opening.

7.6. The receiver at the destination is told in advance by Fleet Control that
the seal was changed on the road, so that the number mismatch is not treated as
a tamper.

## 5. People and shifts

5.1. The site manager is Prakash Jadhav. He is the escalation contact for the
site at any hour and the only person who may approve a change to the van plan
after it has been published.

5.2. The site works three shifts: 06:00 to 14:00, 14:00 to 22:00 and 22:00 to
06:00. Inbound trailers are mostly unloaded on the night shift; outbound vans are
loaded from 04:30 on the morning shift.

5.3. Each shift has a shift lead. Swati Kulkarni leads the morning shift, Imran
Shaikh the afternoon shift, and the night shift lead is named on the weekly
roster on the canteen board, because two people share it.

5.4. Floor labour is supplied under contract by Sai Kripa Manpower. Contract
staff are inducted by the shift lead before their first shift and wear the
green bibs; Quillfern staff wear blue.

5.5. Nobody works inside FC-A for more than 45 minutes without a 15-minute warm
break in the canteen. The shift lead keeps the break board and moves names on
it, not the workers themselves.

5.6. Freezer suits, gloves and boots are issued to named people. A worker without
a suit does not enter FC-A, even for a minute to fetch one carton.

5.7. Overtime is approved by the site manager in advance. A shift that cannot
finish a trailer leaves it for the next shift with a handover note; it does not
stay on past the end of shift to finish it.

## 1. Release

1.1. Release is recorded on form QCL-F-31 and signed by the QA investigator and a second QA officer who did not investigate the case.

1.2. A white RELEASED tag is fixed beside the red hold tag. The red hold tag is never removed; both stay on the stock until it leaves the site.

1.3. Stock is not released between 22:00 and 06:00, whatever the dispatch plan says. The earliest release of the day is at 06:00.

1.4. Released quantity is counted twice by two people and entered separately from any destroyed quantity.

## 3. How long stock may sit

3.1. Quarantine Dwell Limit (QDL) is the time stock may stay in quarantine after the excursion is confirmed before the account manager must escalate to the customer's quality head.

| product class | QDL |
|---|---|

## 12. Paperwork that comes back

12.1. Each trip returns a trip bag holding the dispatch note, the fuel slips,
the cut seals, the takeover sheet and any exception form.

12.2. The trip bag is handed to the shift lead at the returning DC, who checks
it against the dispatch note and signs for it.

12.3. A missing item in the trip bag is written on the dispatch note as
missing, never replaced with a guess. A torn fuel slip is kept torn.

12.4. Trip bags from a trip involving a tyre change or other vendor work carry
the vendor's job sheet with the hours and the spare parts used, so that Fleet
Control can match it to the vendor's invoice.

12.5. Trip bags are kept by Fleet Control for three years, or seven where the
trip involved a pharma critical excursion, a crash, an insurance claim or a
police matter.

|---|---|
| dairy | 12 hours |

| product class | QDL |

3.2. Reaching the QDL does not release anything. It starts an escalation; the stock stays where it is.

## 10. Doors, curtains and ice

10.1. Every door into FC-A and the cell is a rapid-roll door with a strip curtain
behind it. A door that does not close fully within 20 seconds of a vehicle
passing is reported to the shift lead.

10.2. The door heaters keep the frame of each freezer door from icing. The
morning shift lead checks each heater light at the start of the shift and logs
any that is out.

10.3. Ice on the floor in front of a freezer door is chipped and cleared at once,
not left for the next shift. The ice is swept into the drain channel outside,
never left in the anteroom to melt.

10.4. A strip curtain with a torn strip is replaced within a week. The spare
strips are in the store cage in the anteroom.

10.5. The dock seals at D4 to D6 are checked by the guard each evening. A seal
that does not meet the van body lets warm air into the anteroom and frost onto
the picking cartons.

## Flat tyre on a loaded vehicle

The listed tyre vendor should reach a loaded vehicle within 2 hours. Wait with
the vehicle; do not change the tyre yourself.

## 6. Roadside trouble

6.1. A driver whose vehicle develops a fault stops at a safe place first and
calls second. A lit fuel plaza, a toll rest area or a police post is a safe
place; a road shoulder at night is not, unless the vehicle cannot be moved.

6.2. Roadside tyre changes on a loaded reefer are done by the listed tyre
vendor, never by the driver alone, and Fleet Control expects the vendor within
3 hours on a qualified lane.

6.3. A reefer unit fault is reported with the display reading, the alarm code
and the time. Fleet Control decides whether to send the mobile service van,
transfer the load, or bring the vehicle in. The driver does not open the reefer
unit's panel.

6.4. A breakdown on a lane where the fuel pumps are a quarter of a day apart
makes the wait long. Drivers on such lanes carry water and a torch, and the
mobile service van is not always the quickest help; sometimes the relief point
vendor on the lane arrives first.

6.5. A vehicle that cannot be moved and is carrying pharma critical stock is
reported to Compliance-Red by Fleet Control within the SOP's notification
window, whatever the cause.

6.6. After any roadside repair, the vehicle is walked round again before it
moves, as if it were being taken over.

## Closing note

This event is the reason I am asking for two changes: faster pharma escalation
and a shorter vaccine high-duration trigger. If the telematics vendor changes,
the first acceptance test must prove night alerts reach Compliance-Red, not only
the DC manager.

I have deliberately left the rough timeline language in place because the audit
packet should show how the team understood the event on the day. Later SOP
revisions may be cleaner, but this note is the incident record, not a training
poster. Any future reader should compare it with the live SOP before using its
thresholds.

## Impact

The stock was not released on the morning route. BharatVac provided a stability
letter for part of the consignment after reviewing lot data. QA destroyed
13,200 vials and conditionally released 5,200 vials under BharatVac letter
BV-QA-2025-0312. Finance booked a write-off of Rs. 7.82 lakh for the destroyed
vials, packaging, and reverse logistics.

The customer notification was late. Under the incident practice then in use, we
treated customer notice as a same-day item after QA review. That is not
acceptable for patient critical stock. The revised procedure must require
customer notice within two hours after confirmation.

The incident also consumed most of the night shift's available quarantine space.
Two dairy returns were left in the outer holding lane while Q-3 was cleared for
the vaccine pallets. No dairy spoilage was confirmed, but the congestion made
the response slower and showed that pharma critical quarantine cannot depend on
moving unrelated stock at the last minute.

Customer service received three different numbers during the morning: 18,400
vials affected, 13,200 vials destroyed, and 5,200 vials conditionally released.
All three numbers were true in their own context, but the first customer draft
mixed them together. The final notice separated affected quantity, destroyed
quantity, and released quantity.

# Postmortem: Nagpur vaccine excursion, March 2025

This note was written on the afternoon of 12 March 2025 after the C2 cold room
temperature event at Nagpur DC. I am recording the timeline while memories are
fresh. Spelling and header cleanup can wait; evidence cannot.

## Root cause

The immediate cause was warm air ingress through a torn door curtain and door
opening during dairy cross-dock spillover. The deeper cause was that the Kalpa
alert routing still pointed to the old qa-shared mailbox, which was not watched
by the night team. The shift lead tried to protect the room by placing dry ice
near the curtain, but the team did not quarantine stock until the manager was
awake.

We also found that dock scheduling pushed paneer loading next to the vaccine
cold-room door. This did not create the torn curtain, but it increased door
traffic during the vulnerable period. The dock plan must separate pharma
loading from dairy overflow during night shift.

# RC-40 reefer container hire - day rate, minimum hire, empty hold, condenser fan clearance

**From:** Sanjay Mehra <sanjay.mehra@arcticarentals.example>

**To:** Engineering pool <engpool@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Tue, 12 May 2026 11:05:42 +0530

Ravindra,

Confirming our RC-40 reefer container hire terms for this year's season.

Day rate and minimum hire: Rs. 5,500 per day, with a minimum hire of 7 days.
A long hire of 60 days or more is Rs. 4,600 per day.

Empty hold before loading: on arrival the container pulls down to set point
and then holds it empty for 12 hours before any stock goes in. The hold has
been 12 hours since we started renting these units in 2024, and we see no
reason to change it.

Clear space by the condenser fans: keep 1 metre clear beside the condenser
fans. Our crew will not place a container closer than that to a wall.

Delivery and collection are quoted separately per site.

Regards,
Sanjay Mehra
Arctica Rentals, Pune

## 1. The six units

1.1. The pool owns six units, MCR-1 to MCR-6. Each is a 20-foot insulated
container with a refrigeration unit at one end, a personnel door at the other,
internal shelving and a controller that logs the inside temperature every
minute.

1.2. MCR-1 to MCR-4 run at +2 to +8 C and are used for chilled medicine and
chilled food. MCR-5 and MCR-6 can also run at -20 C and are used for frozen
stock or for vaccines that are shipped frozen.

1.3. At any time about four units are out on campaign hires of a few weeks and
two are on long hires. The pool coordinator keeps the deployment board.

1.4. Every unit carries its number on both long sides and on the door. A unit is
never relabelled, even after a refurbishment.

1.5. The units were bought in 2024 and 2025. Their refrigeration units are under
the maker's warranty until the dates written on the inside of each door.

## 7. What a customer pays

7.1. A unit is hired by the day. Charging is Rs. 4,800 a day, and no booking is billed for fewer than 14 days, however early the unit is released.

7.2. A long hire, meaning ninety days or more, is Rs. 3,900 a day.

7.3. Delivery and collection are charged separately at the pool's transport
rate, and the standby genset on a campaign hire is included in the daily
charge.

7.4. The pool coordinator raises the hire invoice monthly in arrears. Fuel for
the genset is the customer's own cost.

7.5. A unit damaged by the customer's people is repaired at the customer's
cost, against the engineer's report and photographs.

7.6. The daily charge stops on the day the unit leaves the customer's site,
not on the day the customer stops using it.

## 10. Emergency cold for a customer's kitchen

10.1. Restaurant chains sometimes ask for emergency dry-ice packing when their
own freezer fails. Customer service takes the request; the DC decides whether it
can be done.

10.2. The agent does not promise a time. The DC tells the agent when the packing
can be ready, and the agent passes that on.

10.3. Emergency dry-ice packing is billed at a minimum of 10 kg per request,
whatever smaller quantity the kitchen asks for, and the per-kg price is the one
on the rate card in force.

10.4. Dry ice is never sent in a customer's own car unless the customer's driver
signs the dry-ice safety note at the gate. Customer service sends the note to
the customer with the confirmation.

10.5. Pharma customers are not offered dry-ice packing as an emergency measure.

## 4. Giving a customer a price

4.1. Agents quote from the rate card in force on the day of the quotation, and
write the rate card's effective date on the quotation.

4.2. BharatVac and Manjara Dairy are never quoted from the rate card. Their
prices come from Finance under their annexes.

4.3. Passive shipper hire is quoted only for consignments that start at Nagpur,
because the shippers are at Nagpur. A shipper cannot be quoted on a Guwahati or
Coimbatore dispatch unless the account manager has arranged for the consignment
to go through Nagpur.

4.4. The Guwahati monsoon handling line is quoted only on Guwahati loads in its
months. It is not added to Coimbatore or Nagpur loads.

4.5. The diesel surcharge is quoted as a rule, not as a figure: the agent writes
the rule from the rate card and lets the invoice apply it on the day of travel.

4.6. Agents do not discount. Any price below the rate card is an account
manager's call, confirmed in writing by Finance.

## 8. Claims

8.1. A customer claim for damaged or lost stock is accepted in writing only,
from a named contact on the account.

8.2. A claim is registered only when it arrives within 30 days of delivery and
carries photographs of the stock and the seal taken at delivery.

8.3. The agent registers the claim, acknowledges it within one working day, and
passes it to the account manager. The agent does not give an opinion on it.

8.4. Stock value in a claim is taken from the Finance schedule. A value in the
customer's email is recorded as the declared value and nothing more.

8.5. A claim that turns on a temperature record waits for QA's investigation.
The customer is told it is waiting, and given the investigation's reference.

8.6. Claims for trips before 18 August 2025 quote the KLP trip number, not a TSL
one.

# Containerised Unit Operating Manual

How the engineering pool's containerised cold rooms are placed, powered,
started, used, moved and looked after. The units are hired out to customers who
need cold space where Quillfern has no building: hospitals running vaccination
campaigns, a dairy cooperative's collection centre in the flush season, a
programme that needs a small store in a city neighbourhood. The manual is for
the engineers who place and service the units and for the customer's people who
use them day to day.

## 13. Records

13.1. The placement sheet, the service cards, the alarm log and the controller
logs are kept for three years, or seven where a temperature alarm was raised
during a pharma hire.

13.2. Controller logs are downloaded at every service visit and at the end of
every hire.

## 11. Cleaning

11.1. The customer's staff wipe the shelves and floor weekly with the cleaner
supplied by the pool. Water is never sprayed inside a unit.

11.2. A unit is deep-cleaned by the pool between every two hires and whenever a
spill has been reported.

11.3. Food and medicine are never in the same unit during one hire.

# Customer Service Handbook

For customer service agents and account managers at Pune HQ and at the three
DCs. It says how customer service works with customers and with the rest of
Quillfern. It sets no temperature limit, no notification window and no price;
those are in the SOP, the customer notification matrix and the rate card, and an
agent opens those documents rather than quoting this handbook.

## 14. Changes to this manual

14.1. Revision 2 (February 2026) lengthened the stability hold after a campaign
unit drifted.

14.2. Revision 3 (July 2026) added the long-hire daily charge and the rule that
a move within a site is a new placement.

14.3. The pool lead reviews this manual every January.

# Postmortem: Nagpur vaccine excursion, March 2025

This note was written on the afternoon of 12 March 2025 after the C2 cold room
temperature event at Nagpur DC. I am recording the timeline while memories are
fresh. Spelling and header cleanup can wait; evidence cannot.

## Summary

At approximately 02:16 on 12 March 2025, Kalpa probe KV-NGP-C2-07 began
reporting a high temperature in C2, the vaccine cold room at Nagpur DC. The
affected consignment was BharatVac order BV-4437, holding 18,400 vials of
rotavirus vaccine in lots ROTA-9A and ROTA-9B. The approved record showed the
room above +8.0 C for 66 minutes. At the time of the event, the SOP required a
QA call after 30 continuous minutes above +8.0 C for vaccines. The current
corrective action is to reduce that duration.

| revision | date | editor | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | 2025-03-14 | Revathi Iyer | Added Nagpur vaccine incident controls and reduced vaccine high duration from 30 minutes to 15 minutes. |

## Closing note

This event is the reason I am asking for two changes: faster pharma escalation
and a shorter vaccine high-duration trigger. If the telematics vendor changes,
the first acceptance test must prove night alerts reach Compliance-Red, not only
the DC manager.

I have deliberately left the rough timeline language in place because the audit
packet should show how the team understood the event on the day. Later SOP
revisions may be cleaner, but this note is the incident record, not a training
poster. Any future reader should compare it with the live SOP before using its
thresholds.

## 2. Products and limits

2.1. Vaccines must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. A vaccine high excursion is
declared when any approved sensor records more than +8.0 C for 15 continuous
minutes. A vaccine low excursion is declared when the record is below +2.0 C
for 10 continuous minutes.

2.2. Insulin must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. An insulin high excursion is
declared when the approved record is more than +8.0 C for 20 continuous
minutes. An insulin low excursion is declared when the record is below +2.0 C
for 10 continuous minutes.

2.3. Milk and paneer must remain from 0.0 C to +4.0 C while in cold rooms and
reefer bodies. A dairy high excursion is declared when milk or paneer is above
+5.0 C for 30 continuous minutes, including staging time after dock release.

2.4. Frozen food must remain at or below -18.0 C. A frozen-food excursion is
declared when the approved record is warmer than -15.0 C for 20 continuous
minutes.

2.5. The Nagpur central hub is also referred to as "NGP hub" in older records.
For this SOP, Nagpur DC and NGP hub mean the same facility unless a customer
contract names a different annex.

2.6. Legacy staging note retained from revision 2.0: milk crates may remain on a
covered dock until +7.0 C for 45 minutes before QA notice is required. This
paragraph has not been relied on since revision 4.0 and is retained only because
customer annex QF-Dairy-11 still quotes it.

## 9. Insulin without spare cold

9.1. Coimbatore holds no passive shippers, no gel packs and no conditioning
cabinet. The passive shipper pilot is at Nagpur only, and it does not extend to
Coimbatore until a later project is approved.

9.2. Because there are no shippers, insulin at Coimbatore is never staged on an
open dock beyond the SOP limit. Insulin moves from CBE-PHARMA straight into a
reefer body that is already at loading temperature, and the reefer waits for
the insulin, never the other way round.

9.3. A customer who asks Coimbatore for a shipper-packed consignment is told
that the site cannot pack one. The account manager may arrange for a
shipper-packed consignment to come from Nagpur.

9.4. Coimbatore does not stock blue-cap or white-cap packs of any kind, and does
not freeze packs in CBE-FROZEN for customers. A customer's own packs returned
with a consignment go back with the customer's return challan.

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

6.4. The two-person figure is lower at Coimbatore than elsewhere because the
path from the shed to the apron crosses the wash pad, which is wet for most of
the day.

6.5. Dry ice never goes into CBE-PHARMA, never into the closed dairy room, and
never into a cab. Unused pellets go back to the chest in the same shift.

## 6. The shed by the wash pad

6.1. Coimbatore buys dry ice for two jobs only: emergency packing for a
restaurant chain whose own freezer has failed, and top-up of a frozen body that
has to wait on the apron.

6.2. The dry-ice chest stands in the open-sided store shed beside the wash pad,
not inside any building. The shed has a roof and no walls on two sides, so
carbon dioxide does not collect there the way it does in a closed store. For
that reason there is no carbon dioxide monitor at Coimbatore. The chest is never
moved indoors, even in heavy rain.

6.3. Supply and handling at Coimbatore:

| item | Coimbatore rule |

| supplier | Kovai Industrial Gases fills the chest with 60 kg every Tuesday |

## Why pellets

Quillfern used to buy dry ice in blocks. Blocks had to be broken with a mallet on the dock, and two hand injuries in 2024 came from exactly that.
The blocks came in 12 kg slabs, and staff carried the slabs by hand because no
tote was used for them. The chest lid has two handles. Vidarbha Gases rated
pellets as easier to meter by the kg, and pellets of 16 mm from Vidarbha Gases
replaced blocks in 2024.

## Why a second pair of hands

The tote handles are rated for 12 kg, so one person with a full tote is already at the limit of the handles.
A dropped tote on a wet dock scatters pellets that people then pick up with the
wrong gloves.

## Why the monitor over the chest

In 2024 a loader felt dizzy after the chest had been left open overnight in the
closed store. The monitor was fitted over the chest that month, so that nobody
has to judge the air by how they feel.

# Dry ice at Quillfern: why the present rules

## Why it stays out of C2 and C3

On the night of 12 March 2025 dry ice trays were set outside the inner curtain
of C2 to hold the room down. The intention was good, but the trays masked the room reading at the curtain and put the vials nearest the door at risk of dropping below +2.0 C.
A pharma room is protected by containment and quarantine, not by cooling it from
the outside.

## Why never in a cab

A driver's cab is small and closed. Pellets left in a cab overnight turn into
gas that the driver then breathes on the road.

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 2. People and phones

2.1. DC manager: S. Venkatesan. He is also the nominated escalation contact for
temperature events at Coimbatore under appendix A of the SOP.

2.2. Shift leads: Kavitha Ramasamy on the morning shift, and Arul Doss on the
afternoon shift. On the security-only night, the senior guard phones the DC
manager, never the shift leads, for anything that is not a fire.

2.3. Security is contracted to Nilgiri Guarding. The senior guard on each night
is named on the security roster pinned in the gate cabin. Guards change every
four weeks, which is why the gate cabin keeps its own copy of every card that
matters to them.

2.4. QA has no officer based at Coimbatore. QA work is done by the shift lead
with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone, extension 440 in business hours. For a
pharma critical event at any hour, the shift lead calls Compliance-Red as at
every other site.

2.5. Fleet Control is in Nagpur on extension 301. Coimbatore has no fleet desk
of its own; the shift lead is Fleet Control's eyes on the apron.

2.6. The site landline goes to the office annexe. After 22:00 it diverts to the
gate cabin, and the guard answers it with the site name only, never with a
person's name.

## 2. Hours and cover

2.1. The Pune desk is staffed from 07:00 to 21:00, Monday to Saturday. On
Sundays and public holidays one agent is on call from home from 07:00 to 21:00.

2.2. From 21:00 to 07:00 there is no customer service agent on duty. A customer
who calls at night reaches a recorded message giving the Fleet Control number
for vehicles on the road and the QA desk number for business hours.

2.3. At night, if a pharma critical excursion is confirmed, QA calls the
customer service lead at home so that the customer notice can be sent inside
the window. The lead's phone is on the Compliance-Red call list for that
reason.

2.4. Agents at the DCs work the DC's day shift. When a DC agent is on leave, the
Pune desk covers that DC's accounts and says so in the customer's ticket.

2.5. Leave is planned so that no account manager and their backup are away in
the same week.

## 13. Language and new people

13.1. Coimbatore works in Tamil. Training is given by a trainer in Tamil, with
English slides available but never used instead of a trainer.

13.2. New joiners spend their first week on the morning shift only. They are not
put on the late shift, and never left alone in the cold block, until a shift
lead has signed them off.

13.3. Every new joiner is shown the gate cabin, the security roster and the key
register on the first day. They are told that security will not open anything
for them at night except in an emergency, and that the lockers, the cabinet and
the seal drawer are all separate keys.

13.4. New drivers from hired-truck vendors are shown the south gate routine by
the guard and the Temple Street timing by the shift lead before their first
booking.

13.5. The words used on site follow the company glossary. A new joiner who hears
a word they do not know is expected to ask, on any shift, and nobody at
Coimbatore is to laugh at the question.

## 17. New agents

17.1. A new agent spends the first two weeks listening to calls with an
experienced agent and reading closed tickets. They do not answer customers alone
in that time.

17.2. In the third week the new agent answers calls with the experienced agent
listening. The experienced agent signs the new agent off when they are ready,
not on a fixed day.

17.3. New agents spend one day at Nagpur DC in their first month, with a shift
lead, so that they have seen a cold room, a dock and a gate before they speak to
customers about them.

17.4. The customer service lead meets each new agent at the end of their first
month and again at three months.

## 10. Doors, curtains and ice

10.1. Every door into FC-A and the cell is a rapid-roll door with a strip curtain
behind it. A door that does not close fully within 20 seconds of a vehicle
passing is reported to the shift lead.

10.2. The door heaters keep the frame of each freezer door from icing. The
morning shift lead checks each heater light at the start of the shift and logs
any that is out.

10.3. Ice on the floor in front of a freezer door is chipped and cleared at once,
not left for the next shift. The ice is swept into the drain channel outside,
never left in the anteroom to melt.

10.4. A strip curtain with a torn strip is replaced within a week. The spare
strips are in the store cage in the anteroom.

10.5. The dock seals at D4 to D6 are checked by the guard each evening. A seal
that does not meet the van body lets warm air into the anteroom and frost onto
the picking cartons.

## 10. Seal books and the security cabin

10.1. Seal books for Coimbatore are issued by Stores at Nagpur and arrive by
courier two books at a time. They are kept in the locked drawer in the gate
cabin, not in the office annexe, because the gate cabin is staffed all night and
the annexe is not.

10.2. Only one seal book is open at the gate at a time. The guard hands a seal
to the shift lead; the guard never fits a seal himself.

10.3. The rest of the sealing rule is the company rule. Seal numbers go on the
dispatch note and in QCL-F-35 before the vehicle moves.

10.4. A vehicle arriving with a broken seal or a number that does not match is
kept outside the south gate, photographed, and reported to Fleet Control before
anyone opens the doors.

the slot and the products.

5.2. The patient receives an SMS with the slot and a one-time code the evening
before, and a second SMS when the rider leaves the hub.

5.3. At the door the rider asks for the OTP. The patient reads out the four-figure code sent by SMS; without it nothing is handed over.

5.4. A patient who has lost the SMS is asked to call the Nirmaya care desk, which
can resend the code. The rider does not accept a name, a photograph or a
neighbour's word instead.

5.5. Slots that the hub cannot meet are moved by the hub lead, never by the
rider, and the patient is called before the original slot begins.

5.6. Nirmaya may book a same-day slot only before 13:00. Same-day bookings after
13:00 go into the next morning.

# Sahyog doorstep insulin delivery - OTP code, waiting at the door, neighbour handover

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who

front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

## Leaving insulin with a neighbour or watchman

If the patient is out, the insulin may be left with a neighbour or the building watchman, as long as that person shows photo ID and signs the delivery slip.

## 9. Pay

9.1. Riders are paid a monthly wage for their shifts, with a small per-drop

9.2. There is no payment for early arrival and no penalty for a drop that comes

9.3. Fuel for the two-wheelers is paid by Quillfern through a fuel card. Riders

9.4. Overtime is paid at the company rate and approved by the hub lead before

# Quillfern Cold Chain Glossary

Plain meanings for expressions used on site. Short forms are defined in the document that uses them, never here, so an expression below appears in its long form only.

back-to-cold — the moment a staged pallet crosses back over the cold-room threshold; staging time stops here.
chlorine contact time — the minutes a sanitising solution must stay wet on a reefer floor before rinsing; wiping it dry early starts the count again.
dead zone — a stretch of road where the telematics unit cannot report; the USB logger covers it and the gap is recorded as missing, never filled in.
door open minutes — the total minutes a cold-room or reefer door stood open in one shift, summed from the door sensor; a measure of load, not a fault.
holding lane B — the covered waiting lane at Nagpur for pharma and frozen vehicles that miss their dock time; nothing is unloaded there.
mean kinetic temperature — the single steady temperature that would give stock the same total heat stress as the uneven record it actually saw; stability letters are written against it, not against the average.
pre-cool hold time — the minutes an empty reefer body is held at loading temperature, doors shut, before the first pallet goes in.
probe grid — the layout of loggers used when a room is mapped; each position is named by rack, bay and height, such as A1-high.
relief point — a named fuel plaza or rest area on a qualified route where a relief driver or a mobile service van can meet the vehicle.
seal watch — time a driver spends guarding a sealed vehicle; it is duty time and never counts as rest.
shipper conditioning time — the hours a passive shipper's gel packs must sit at their set temperature before the shipper may leave with stock.
stability budget remaining — the minutes above the high limit that a customer's stability letter still allows for one lot, once every earlier excursion on that lot is subtracted.
warm pallet — night-shift name for a pallet whose logger has alarmed but whose excursion QA has not yet confirmed; it is handled as quarantine stock until QA decides.
white tag — the RELEASED tag fixed beside a red hold tag when QA lets stock out of quarantine; the red tag stays on.

## Before loading

1. Two drivers are named on the dispatch note before departure, as clause 2.3 of the [Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md) requires.

2. The body is run empty with its doors shut until the display holds loading temperature, and then held there for the Pre-Cool Hold Time (PCH) set by the qualification record for that route. Where no qualification record exists, the PCH is 45 minutes.

3. The red sleeve is in the cab locker and holds a spare calibrated logger. No logger, no departure: a hand-held thermometer is not a substitute.

4. Where the qualification record requires a backup passive shipper, its SCT is written in the shipper register. A shipper with no SCT entry is not a backup and the run waits.

## 5. Temperatures

5.1. The customer's products are kept at -18 C or colder in storage and in
transit.

5.2. The customer pre-cools each trailer before loading at Chakan and sends the
pre-cool record with the trailer.

5.3. Product that turns up above minus 12 is brought down to temperature at the cross-dock, and that work is invoiced to the customer.

5.4. Quillfern is not liable for product damage caused by temperatures before
handover. Each party may inspect the other's temperature records for its
stock.

# Pharma Critical Night Dispatch Checklist

Worked through at the gate by the Fleet controller and the shift lead together before any pharma critical vehicle leaves a Quillfern DC between 22:00 and 05:00. Both sign. One signature is not a dispatch.

## 4. Product, packing and handover

4.1. The customer packs its products in cartons that carry the batch number and
the best-before date on two faces.

4.2. Loaded pallets stand no higher than 1.8 metres including the wooden base. Taller pallets are restacked at the customer's cost before they are
accepted.

4.3. Each pallet is stretch-wrapped and labelled with the customer's pallet ID
on two faces.

4.4. Handover takes place when the pallet crosses the dock edge at the
receiving site. The receiving shift lead's count is the count.

## 3. Commitments on both sides

3.1. The customer commits to 1,800 pallet movements in each calendar month; any month that falls short is charged Rs. 300 for each movement not made.

3.2. A pallet movement is one pallet received or one pallet dispatched. A pallet
received and dispatched in the same month counts twice.

3.3. Quillfern commits to hold enough frozen space in Pune for 900 of the
customer's pallets at any one time, and to give 30 days' notice before reducing
it.

3.4. Months in which Quillfern could not take the customer's stock, for reasons
on Quillfern's side, are not counted for the shortfall charge.

## 12. Insurance

12.1. Quillfern insures the customer's stock in its care up to the contract-year
total in section 7.2.

12.2. The customer insures its stock before handover and after delivery.

## 13. Audit and records

13.1. The customer may audit the records about its own stock twice a year on

13.2. Records are kept for three years after the end of the agreement.
